FIXED 2026-09-14. The read-then-increment collision is now serialised: append, import-flat, dedupe and resolve take journal/.lock (O_CREAT|O_EXCL) for the whole read-compute-write section and refuse with exit 3 if another session holds it, breaking a lock older than 600s so a crashed session cannot wedge the journal. Evidence: the defect fired for real before the fix, producing 217 collided ids and 60 duplicate-id ERRORs in check; the repair tool (dedupe, which suffixes the later copy exactly as the migration did) restored 718 entries with 718 distinct ids and 0 errors; all three lock cases were then tested (live lock refuses, stale lock breaks and releases, read-only commands unaffected). Residual: this is a per-tree lock, so it cannot serialise two machines that pull and push independently - only a single tree's writers - and the allocation is still read-then-increment rather than allocated at merge time. The larger instance of that residual is recorded separately as P72.

RESOLVED 2026-09-14, measured on the SHARED repo not locally: git ls-tree over origin/master's journal/log shards counts 723 entry markers and origin/master's index has 723 rows, exactly matching the local tree's 723. The ~230 entries that existed only in working copies are now distributed, via fast-forward pushes onto master once the shared working tree had advanced onto origin/master. Residual, named so it is not mistaken for solved: the count agreeing today does not make the mechanism safe. Ids are still allocated at write time from refs the writer has fetched, so two machines pulling and pushing independently can still collide; what prevents it is journal.py dedupe (repairs collisions without losing content) and the per-tree lock (stops two writers in one tree). Both are on master. A merge-time allocator, or a single allocating authority, would be the structural fix and is not built.

Verified 245,897 -> 17,643 bytes, ps_health 385,651 -> 27,350. Commit 33bc517e, seven tests, every caller checked first.
